newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Zeitler sees no reason for rate cut now.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Zeitler sees no reason for rate cut now.

text.p: Germany's low inflation levels but relatively strong money supply growth currently prompt the central bank to leave interest rates unchanged, senior Bundesbank official Franz-Christoph Zeitler said on Tuesday.

"There are neither impending inflationary dangers that would make a rate hike necessary nor do I see reasons for a rate cut in light of the strong growth in money supply and the impact of the foreign exchange situation's impact on import prices," Zeitler said in a statement.
Zeitler, also president of the state central bank in Bavaria, will deliver a speech in the town of Cham, near the Czech border, this evening. His office made the statement available ahead of time.
Zeitler also said that since German interest rates were currently at historic lows they did not "post an obstacle to growth and employment."

The Bundesbank last cut its interest rates in April 1996, moving the discount rate to 2.50 percent and the Lombard rate to 4.50 percent. The main money market rate has been steady at three percent since August, 1996.
On Monday, Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke also said that there were no reasons for the central bank to veer away from its so-called "steady hand policy" at this moment.

Turning to the capital markets, Zeitler said that in light of current price stability, Germany's efforts to consolidate its finances and sluggish economic growth, cheap financing conditions would last for some time.
But Zeitler also said that international factors could lead to a "blip in capital market rates".

Touching on Europe's planned monetary union, Zeitler said "while it (EMU) will not promise to be a panacea able to gloss over structural problems in a pain-free manner, it would create a medium and long-term strengthening of the economy".
The currency union's benefits would, however, be directly impacted by the way in which nations interpret and uphold the spirit of the Maastricht Treaty, Zeitler said.

"Benefits will be better seen the more convergent the economic development in member nations," Zeitler said, adding it was similarly important for the stability and credibility criteria in the Maastricht Treaty to be upheld.

Germany's central bank officials have recently stepped up their efforts to convince a sceptical German public that the currency union would have distinct benefits so long as nations meet the strict stability-oriented entry criteria.

The currency union is scheduled to begin in January, 1999 with as many nations as meet the criteria. Next year, Europe's political leaders will determine which nations meet the criteria and will be allowed to enter.
